lessons.title: Building and Backtesting a Simple Order Book Imbalance Signal on Nifty Futures

body.text: A signal that looks great on paper and a signal that would have actually made money are separated entirely by backtesting discipline. Every concept this course has built, from order book imbalance to VPIN to Kyle's lambda, is worthless without an honest, leak-free test of whether it was ever really tradeable.

children.text: Defining the Signal: OBI With a VPIN Filter

This lesson builds one deliberately simple signal on Nifty futures out of two pieces from this chapter: multi-level order book imbalance as the directional read, and VPIN as a gate that steps aside precisely when conditions look most informed. That combination is a specific, defensible design choice, not the only reasonable one. A retail-scale researcher without colocation, per the previous lesson's honest assessment, is poorly positioned to compete for queue position exactly when VPIN signals elevated toxicity, so the signal trades OBI's directional edge in calmer conditions and deliberately avoids the regime this course has repeatedly flagged as requiring infrastructure it does not assume you have.

Compute multi-level OBI, from Lesson 1, over the top three depth levels every second, and VPIN, from Lesson 2, over a rolling window of volume buckets, tracking its own recent percentile rather than an absolute level. Go long when OBI exceeds +0.4 and VPIN sits below its own 80th percentile; go short on the mirror condition, OBI below -0.4 with VPIN still below that same percentile. Exit a position after a fixed 30-second holding period or immediately if OBI flips sign, whichever comes first. Every threshold here, 0.4, the 80th percentile, 30 seconds, is a reasonable starting choice, not a number pulled from a validated study, and the biases section below explains exactly why that distinction matters.

Chapter 1 opened this course with a trader whose correct call still lost money to execution. A backtest that does not charge for the same costs that trader paid is not a backtest of anything tradeable, it is a description of a world that does not exist. Every simulated trade here pays at least half the quoted spread on entry and exit, plus a price impact estimate from Kyle's lambda scaled to the position size, both covered in Chapter 3. Skipping either cost is the single most common way a promising-looking signal turns out to be an illusion.

body.code:
def backtest_obi_signal(bars, obi_threshold=0.4, vpin_pct_threshold=0.80,
                         hold_seconds=30, half_spread=0.05, impact_lambda=0.05):
    """
    bars: sequence of rows with ['timestamp', 'price', 'obi', 'vpin_percentile'].
    Execution always happens on the NEXT bar after a signal forms on the
    current bar, never on the same bar, to avoid look-ahead bias.
    """
    position = 0
    entry_price = None
    entry_time = None
    trades = []

    for i in range(len(bars) - 1):
        row = bars[i]
        next_row = bars[i + 1]  # execution on the next bar, not this one

        # Exit: fixed holding period or a signal flip, whichever comes first
        if position != 0:
            held = (row['timestamp'] - entry_time).total_seconds()
            flipped = (position == 1 and row['obi'] < 0) or (position == -1 and row['obi'] > 0)
            if held >= hold_seconds or flipped:
                exit_price = next_row['price']
                cost = half_spread + impact_lambda  # simple two-sided cost model
                pnl = position * (exit_price - entry_price) - cost
                trades.append(pnl)
                position = 0

        # Entry: only when flat, using this bar's already-known OBI and VPIN
        if position == 0:
            if row['obi'] > obi_threshold and row['vpin_percentile'] < vpin_pct_threshold:
                position = 1
                entry_price = next_row['price']
                entry_time = next_row['timestamp']
            elif row['obi'] < -obi_threshold and row['vpin_percentile'] < vpin_pct_threshold:
                position = -1
                entry_price = next_row['price']
                entry_time = next_row['timestamp']

    return trades
body.caption: A deliberately minimal backtest loop. The signal is read from the current bar, but every execution price comes from the next bar, and every trade pays a two-sided cost before its P&L is recorded.

markDefs.definition: A backtesting error where a simulated decision uses information that would not actually have been available at that moment in real time, such as computing a signal from a bar and then trading at that same bar's own price instead of the next one.

children.text: The Three Ways This Kind of Backtest Lies to You

body.caption: Three failure modes that turn a backtest into fiction

cells: Using the same bar's price to both compute the signal and enter the trade, or computing VPIN with buckets that include data after the decision moment
Always execute on the bar after a signal forms; recompute every input using only data strictly before the decision timestamp
Trying every OBI cutoff from 0.1 to 0.9 and every holding period from 5 to 120 seconds, then reporting only the best combination found
Choose thresholds from a single reasonable prior, or split data into separate in-sample and out-of-sample periods and validate the chosen thresholds only on the held-out period
Showcasing the one session or instrument where the strategy performed best, the exact trap Chapter 3's single-session case study warned against
Test across many instruments and many non-overlapping time periods, and report the full distribution of results, not the best case

children.text: Evaluating Results Honestly: Gross vs Net

The single most important comparison in any microstructure backtest is the same result computed twice, once ignoring transaction costs and once charging them properly. The gap between the two is not a rounding error, it is very often the entire difference between a strategy worth pursuing and one that only ever worked on paper.

body.text: The gross and net figures above are illustrative, meant to show the typical shape of cost drag on a short-horizon signal, not results from an actual backtest run on real NSE data. A real result requires running this exact discipline, no look-ahead, honest costs, out-of-sample validation, on genuine historical order book data, which is the natural next step beyond this course rather than something this lesson claims to have already done.

children.text: From Backtest to the Next Step

Even a signal that survives honest, out-of-sample backtesting is not yet a live strategy. The next steps, paper trading against real-time data to confirm the backtest's assumptions hold up outside historical data, and, if ever run with real capital through automated order routing, the SEBI and exchange algo registration process flagged back in Chapter 1, both sit outside what this course covers. What this course has built is the layer underneath all of that: reading the book, understanding why spreads and liquidity behave the way they do, classifying flow, measuring price impact, and turning all of it into a signal you know how to test honestly rather than one you simply hope works.

body.title: A Backtest Report That Looks Too Good
body.scenario: A researcher shows you a backtest of an OBI-based strategy on Nifty futures reporting a Sharpe ratio of 2.1. When you ask, they confirm the backtest does not deduct any transaction costs, and that the signal is computed using each bar's closing price, with trades also entered at that same bar's closing price.
body.prompt: Identify the specific problems with this backtest, using the concepts from this lesson, and explain what a corrected version would need to do differently.
body.modelAnswer: There are two separate, serious problems, not one. First, entering trades at the same bar's closing price that was used to compute the signal is a textbook case of look-ahead bias, since in live trading the signal could only be computed after that price was already known, and the actual entry would have to happen afterward, at whatever price the market had moved to by then. Second, reporting a Sharpe ratio with no transaction costs deducted at all ignores exactly the spread and price impact costs Chapter 1 through Chapter 3 spent building tools to quantify, and this lesson's illustrative gross-to-net comparison shows how large that gap typically is. A corrected version would execute every trade on the bar after the signal forms, not the same bar, and would deduct at minimum a half-spread cost on both entry and exit plus a price impact estimate from Kyle's lambda, then report the Sharpe ratio net of both, which is the only version of that number worth trusting.

body.title: Spotting Selection Bias
body.question: A researcher backtests an OBI-based signal across 40 different trading sessions, finds it performed best on 3 of them, and presents only those 3 sessions' results as evidence the strategy works. What is the clearest problem with this presentation?
options: There is no problem, since the strategy did genuinely perform well on those 3 sessions
This is look-ahead bias, since the researcher already knows the outcome of those 3 sessions
This is selection bias, since showcasing only the best-performing subset of results misrepresents the strategy's typical, honest performance across all 40 sessions
This is overfitting, since the strategy's thresholds were tuned separately for each of the 3 sessions
body.explanation: The strategy's rules were presumably fixed and applied identically across all 40 sessions, so this is not overfitting of thresholds, and knowing a historical outcome after the fact is normal for any backtest, not look-ahead bias specifically. The actual problem is that reporting only the 3 best sessions out of 40 hides the other 37, giving a completely distorted picture of what this strategy's honest, full-sample performance actually looks like, exactly the selection bias this lesson's table warns against.

points: A simple OBI-with-VPIN-filter signal combines this chapter's directional and risk-overlay tools into one testable rule set, without needing colocation-grade infrastructure
A backtest must execute on the bar after a signal forms, never the same bar, or it silently uses information that would not have been available in real time
Every simulated trade needs an honest transaction cost, at minimum a half-spread on each side plus a Kyle's lambda price impact estimate, or the result describes a world that does not exist
Look-ahead bias, overfitting thresholds to a single sample, and selection bias toward the best-performing subset of data are the three most common ways a backtest misleads its own author
The gap between gross and net-of-cost performance is very often the entire difference between a strategy worth pursuing and one that only ever worked on paper

Even an honest, out-of-sample backtest is not a finished trading system; paper trading and, for any live automated execution, SEBI and exchange algo registration remain necessary steps beyond what this course covers
